questions.q: A company issued 50,000 shares of ₹10 each at par, payable as ₹3 on application, ₹3 on allotment, ₹2 on first call, and ₹2 on final call. All money was received except the final call on 2,000 shares. What is the amount of Calls in Arrears and how is it presented in the Balance Sheet?
questions.a: Calls in Arrears = 2,000 shares × ₹2 (final call) = ₹4,000. In the Balance Sheet under 'Share Capital', it is shown as a deduction from Subscribed and Called-up Capital: "Subscribed Capital: 50,000 shares of ₹10 each = ₹5,00,000; Less: Calls in Arrears (₹4,000) = ₹4,96,000". A wrong answer (e.g., showing it as a Current Liability or netting it against Calls in Advance) reveals the student confuses the nature of arrears (unpaid capital, reducing equity) with advance calls (liability).

questions.q: A shareholder holding 500 shares of ₹100 each paid the first and final call of ₹20 per share along with the allotment money. The company's Articles authorise interest on Calls in Advance at 12% p.a. The time gap between allotment and first call due date is 3 months. Calculate the interest on Calls in Advance and state whether it is an income or expense for the company.
questions.a: Calls in Advance = 500 shares × ₹20 = ₹10,000. Interest = ₹10,000 × 12% × 3/12 = ₹300. It is an EXPENSE for the company (interest paid to shareholder for early payment). A wrong answer calculating interest on the full ₹100 per share or treating it as income reveals misunderstanding: interest is only on the advance portion (₹20), not the entire share value, and it is a cost to the company for using shareholder's money early.

questions.q: X Ltd. issued 20,000 shares of ₹10 each. The amount was payable as ₹3 on application, ₹4 on allotment, and ₹3 on first and final call. Applications were received for 25,000 shares; excess application money was adjusted towards allotment. A shareholder holding 1,000 shares paid the call money with allotment. Another shareholder holding 500 shares failed to pay the call. The Articles provide for interest on Calls in Arrears at 10% p.a. and on Calls in Advance at 12% p.a. The call was made on 1st October 2023 and the final accounts are prepared on 31st March 2024. Pass journal entries for: (a) Call money due, (b) Receipt of call money including advance, (c) Calls in Arrears, (d) Interest on Calls in Arrears, (e) Interest on Calls in Advance.
questions.a:
(a) Share First & Final Call A/c Dr. 60,000 To Share Capital A/c 60,000 (Call money due on 20,000 shares @ ₹3)
(b) Bank A/c Dr. 57,000 To Share First & Final Call A/c 57,000 (Received: 18,500 shares × ₹3 = ₹55,500 + Advance 1,000 shares × ₹3 = ₹3,000; Total ₹58,500? Wait — 20,000 shares issued, 500 shares arrears, so 19,500 shares paid call. Of these, 1,000 shares paid in advance earlier, so 18,500 shares paid now. Bank receives 18,500 × ₹3 = ₹55,500. But the 1,000 advance shares already paid ₹3,000 at allotment. So total call money accounted: ₹55,500 + ₹3,000 = ₹58,500. Call due was ₹60,000. Arrears = ₹1,500. So Bank Dr. ₹55,500, Calls in Advance Dr. ₹3,000? No — Calls in Advance was credited at allotment. At call date, we debit Calls in Advance and credit Share Call A/c. Let me restructure:
At allotment: Bank Dr. (includes advance) → Calls in Advance Cr. ₹3,000.
At call date: Share Call A/c Dr. ₹60,000 → Share Capital Cr. ₹60,000.
Then: Bank Dr. ₹55,500 (from 18,500 shares), Calls in Advance Dr. ₹3,000 → Share Call A/c Cr. ₹58,500.
Calls in Arrears: Calls in Arrears A/c Dr. ₹1,500 → Share Call A/c Cr. ₹1,500.
(c) Calls in Arrears A/c Dr. 1,500 To Share First & Final Call A/c 1,500
(d) Interest on Calls in Arrears: Shareholder A/c Dr. 75 To Interest on Calls in Arrears A/c 75 (₹1,500 × 10% × 6/12)
(e) Interest on Calls in Advance: Interest on Calls in Advance A/c Dr. 180 To Shareholder A/c 180 (₹3,000 × 12% × 6/12)
A wrong entry (e.g., crediting Interest on Calls in Advance to P&L directly, or calculating interest on wrong base/period) reveals confusion about: (i) Calls in Advance is a liability adjusted at call date, (ii) Interest on arrears is income (credited to P&L), interest on advance is expense (debited to P&L), (iii) Period calculation from call date to Balance Sheet date.

questions.q: Compare the Balance Sheet disclosure of Calls in Arrears and Calls in Advance as per Schedule III. A student argues: "Both relate to share capital, so they should be netted off and shown as a single line item under Shareholders' Funds." Evaluate this argument with reference to the Companies Act 2013 and Schedule III.
questions.a: The argument is INCORRECT. Schedule III mandates separate disclosure: Calls in Arrears is shown as a deduction from 'Subscribed Capital' under 'Shareholders' Funds' (Note to Share Capital), reducing paid-up capital. Calls in Advance is shown under 'Current Liabilities' → 'Other Current Liabilities' as 'Calls in Advance'. They represent fundamentally different claims: Arrears = unpaid capital (equity reduction); Advance = money received for future calls (liability). Netting them off would misstate both equity and liabilities. A student who agrees reveals a conceptual gap: they treat both as 'adjustments to share capital' rather than understanding arrears reduces owners' claim while advance creates a company obligation.

questions.q: A company's Articles of Association are silent on interest on Calls in Arrears and Calls in Advance. The company charges 10% p.a. on arrears and pays 12% p.a. on advance. Is this permissible under the Companies Act 2013? Justify your answer with the relevant statutory provision.
questions.a: No, it is NOT permissible. Under Table F of Schedule I of the Companies Act 2013 (which applies when Articles are silent): (i) Interest on Calls in Arrears cannot exceed 10% p.a. — the company may charge UP TO 10%, so 10% is allowed. (ii) Interest on Calls in Advance cannot exceed 12% p.a. — the company may pay UP TO 12%, so 12% is allowed. However, the company MUST have Articles authorising such interest; if Articles are silent, Table F applies by default. So charging 10% on arrears and paying 12% on advance IS permissible under Table F defaults. A student who says "not allowed because Articles are silent" misunderstands: Table F provides default provisions that apply automatically when Articles don't specify otherwise. A student who says "any rate is allowed" misses the statutory ceilings.

questions.q: Create a realistic scenario where a company has BOTH Calls in Arrears and Calls in Advance simultaneously. Design a Balance Sheet extract (Share Capital note and Current Liabilities) showing correct presentation with imaginary but plausible figures. Include interest accrued on both as on Balance Sheet date.
questions.a:
Scenario: Y Ltd. issued 1,00,000 shares of ₹10 each (₹3 application, ₹3 allotment, ₹2 first call, ₹2 final call). Final call made 1 Oct 2023. Balance Sheet 31 Mar 2024.
- 1,000 shares: final call unpaid → Calls in Arrears ₹2,000
- 500 shares: final call paid with first call → Calls in Advance ₹1,000
- Interest on Arrears @10% p.a. for 6 months = ₹100 (Income, shown under 'Other Income' in P&L, receivable shown under 'Other Current Assets')
- Interest on Advance @12% p.a. for 6 months = ₹60 (Expense, shown under 'Finance Costs' in P&L, payable shown under 'Other Current Liabilities')

Balance Sheet Extract:
**Shareholders' Funds**
Share Capital:
Authorised: 1,50,000 shares of ₹10 = ₹15,00,000
Issued: 1,00,000 shares of ₹10 = ₹10,00,000
Subscribed & Called-up: 1,00,000 shares of ₹10 = ₹10,00,000
Less: Calls in Arrears (1,000 shares × ₹2) = (₹2,000)
Paid-up Capital = ₹9,98,000

**Current Liabilities**
Other Current Liabilities:
Calls in Advance (500 shares × ₹2) = ₹1,000
Interest Accrued on Calls in Advance = ₹60

**Current Assets**
Other Current Assets:
Interest Accrued on Calls in Arrears = ₹100

A poor answer (e.g., netting arrears and advance, showing interest on arrears as liability, or omitting interest accruals) reveals inability to integrate multiple concepts: Schedule III presentation, interest computation, accrual accounting, and P&L classification.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Calls in Arrears refers to the amount of call money not paid by ______ by the due date, shown as a deduction from Subscribed Capital in the Balance Sheet.
Fill in the blank: Imagine a company issues 10,000 shares of ₹100 each, payable as ₹30 on ______, ₹30 on allotment, ₹20 on first call, and ₹20 on final call.
What is Calls in Arrears? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Calls in Arrears refers to the amount of call money not paid by shareholders by the due date, shown as a deduction from Subscribed Capital in the Balance Sheet.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Calls in Arrears?
questions.a: Students often treat Calls in Arrears as a Current Asset (like a receivable) because "the company will collect it later." They also net off Calls in Arrears against Calls in Advance, showing a single net figure in Shareholders' Funds.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) Calculate Calls in Arrears and Calls in Advance from given share issue data with multiple call stages, (2) Prepare the Share Capital note in Balance Sheet as per Schedule III showing correct presentation of both items, (3) Compute interest on Calls in Arrears (income) and Calls in Advance (expense) at.
